source_neutral.procedure: Examine the checkout request-serving system over a window spanning before and after the regression onset to estimate which component, code segment, configuration or dependency call contributes added delay. The internal distribution of added delay is not directly observed. No single measurement identifies the delay contributed by a particular change; measurements describe requests traversing different paths. Construct a pre-regression reference model of segment delays conditional on load, inspect whether request coverage distinguishes candidate changes, and fit competing explanations of post-regression residuals using changed-unit delay increments, altered load response, or both. Assess estimates using held-out path classes, variation in regularisation and recovery of an introduced synthetic delay. Where coverage cannot distinguish candidates, obtain additional path coverage through specified interventions. Bound causal contribution through removal and reintroduction of the change at comparable load or under representative replay.
source_neutral.action: 1. Use per-request end-to-end latency and, where available, per-span durations. Do not use aggregated percentiles for path summation because percentiles do not add along a path. 2. From the pre-regression window, estimate expected per-traversal delay for each segment as a function of load covariates. Predict each request's latency by summing those segment delays over its traversals, evaluated at the load it experienced. 3. Before estimating delay increments, build and inspect a coverage matrix whose rows are path classes, columns are candidate segment-by-version/configuration units, and entries are traversal counts. Record which candidates have distinct sets of traversing paths, which are always traversed together, and the load strata in which each is sampled. 4. For post-regression requests, subtract the reference-model prediction at observed load from observed latency to obtain residuals. 5. Iteratively adjust the model to reduce residuals, fitting three competing forms: delay increments on changed units; a load-response change without unit increments; and both together. State the regularisation explicitly, including any preference for few changed units, and repeat estimation with weaker and stronger settings. 6. Test whether the procedure can distinguish the location and magnitude of added delay by introducing a known synthetic delay into a chosen unit in recorded data or in replay or staging, with the same path coverage and sampling. Apply the identical estimation procedure and record whether it recovers the correct unit and magnitude or assigns the delay partly or wholly to neighboring units or the load term.
source_neutral.observables: Measure per-request end-to-end latency and available span durations, together with path identity, build version, configuration or flag state, serving host or zone, request rate, concurrency, queue depth and resource utilisation. Examine residual structure across path classes rather than overall residual size. If a deployed change is responsible, the expected pattern is concentration on paths traversing one changed unit; approximate scaling with that unit's traversal count; persistence within matched load strata, including low load; near-zero residuals on paths bypassing the unit at the same load and time window; and onset on each host or instance aligned with its receipt of the change rather than a traffic-level shift. If load variation is responsible, the expected pattern is residuals tracking load covariates across paths sharing the loaded resource regardless of whether they traverse a changed unit, appearing on instances running the old version, and shrinking or vanishing within matched load strata. Residuals restricted to paths traversing a changed unit but increasing with load indicate altered load sensitivity rather than fixed added delay. Residuals without organisation by path or load indicate measurement noise or a missing model component. Also record the recovered location and magnitude of synthetic delay, movement of fitted increments across regularisation settings, and whether intervention removes and restores the residual with the change at held load.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Residual patterns support a constrained estimate of the distribution of added delay, not proof of a unique cause. The supportable statement specifies that, within covered path classes and load strata, an increment of an estimated size with a stated interval in a particular unit reduces residuals to the pre-regression residual spread, while a model with a load-response change and no unit increment does not. If that alternative performs equally well, make no attribution. A change is a supported candidate only when its unit has separately distinguishing coverage, the synthetic-delay test recovers a delay in that unit, and its estimate is stable across regularisation settings. Distinction from load rests on residual persistence at matched load, absence on bypassing and old-version paths at the same load, and onset aligned with the change's arrival on each instance. For the mixed pattern, conclude that the change altered load response and attribute the regression to the change conditional on load, without apportioning it between change and load. If candidate coverage is collinear, the supported statement is that one or more changes in that set account for the estimated delay. Estimation from request records is observational. Causal contribution is bounded only after removing and reintroducing the change at held load, or under representative replay, removes and restores the residual. Report the fraction of the regression in covered paths accounted for by that intervention and report the remainder as unexplained.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: A request path class is the ordered set of segments traversed, including the entry endpoint, service hops, dependency calls and traversal counts. Each class carries build-version, configuration or flag-state, and serving-host or zone identities, together with contemporaneous load conditions. A segment-by-version/configuration unit receives an estimated per-traversal delay; units affected by deployed changes are the candidate locations of added delay. Predicted request latency is the sum of expected delays for its segment traversals at observed load. Load variation is represented separately and changes delay on paths using a loaded shared resource whether or not those paths traverse a changed unit. The coverage matrix relates path classes to candidate units through traversal counts. Distinct coverage provides information for separating candidates; units always traversed together remain jointly constrained. Load strata provide conditional comparisons, and held-out path classes assess residuals beyond the classes used for fitting.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: Check the stated prerequisites before using the procedure. Where existing coverage cannot separate candidates, obtain new request paths instead of continuing to refit the existing coverage. Specified options are a canary carrying a single change, a flag flip on a traffic subset, or bisected builds under replayed representative workload at matched load. Where safe, follow with rollback and controlled reintroduction of the change associated with the indicated unit while keeping load comparable. Observe whether the residual disappears and returns, and use that intervention to bound the accounted-for fraction of the regression.
source_neutral.limits: The packet does not establish the prerequisites: per-request records must carry path and version/configuration identity through traces or joinable logs; a pre-regression window with comparable instrumentation must exist; and there must be more than one candidate change, with at least some requests traversing different candidate subsets, such as through mixed rollout versions, flag-gated subsets or request types that skip a changed segment. If the differing-coverage prerequisite fails, observational data cannot separate candidates. Stop iterating when residuals on held-out path classes are no larger than the pre-regression residual spread, or when further adjustment no longer reduces held-out residuals. Stop without naming a single change when leading candidates have collinear coverage or the synthetic-delay test fails to recover the introduced delay. Sparse or uneven coverage from trace sampling, tail-biased sampling and low-traffic classes leaves units poorly constrained. Changes shipped together and traversed by the same paths cannot be separated. Measurement limitations include clock skew between services, missing or coarse spans, asynchronous work absent from spans, and retries counted as single requests. Path and version assignments may be uncertain because of rolling deployments, imprecise deployment timestamps or cached configuration. A regularisation preference for a single changed unit can produce a single-candidate estimate; smoothing can distribute a localised delay across neighboring units or into the load term. Additive segment-delay assumptions fail with parallel calls, queueing and contention; load response is nonlinear near saturation; tail latency does not decompose additively; and a reference model fitted in one load range may not extrapolate. Several delay distributions or a load-response change may fit equally well. A deployment coinciding with a traffic shift remains confounded. Caches, autoscaling, data growth and dependency behaviour can change during measurement and make the pre-regression reference stale. Timeouts, retries and load balancing can make path selection depend on latency. Staging or replay may not reproduce production data shape or concurrency. Rollback may be unsafe or fail to cleanly remove a change, including with schema or data migrations. Residual disappearance after rollback may coincide with a load change unless load is held or matched. Conclusions apply to the covered paths, load strata and time window. Withdraw or narrow them if the synthetic-delay test fails, estimates shift materially across regularisation settings, or intervention does not reproduce the effect.
